analysis.one_liner: Lets people demand deletion of personal data collected about them online before they turned 13.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee but never received a vote, expiring when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the 1998 children's online privacy law to give people a "right to be forgotten" for their childhood. Anyone over 13 — or their guardian — could ask a website aimed at children to permanently delete all personal information collected about them before they turned 13, and the site would have to confirm the deletion in writing. The Federal Trade Commission would write the rules, and state attorneys general could enforce the new right. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who spent their childhood online. The bill would let adults erase the data trails websites collected about them as children — profiles, activity records, and personal details gathered by sites aimed at kids — before those records can shape advertising, scoring, or other decisions about them later in life. Guardians could act on behalf of people over 13, and state attorneys general could sue on their behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose childhood data is held online

how_it_helps.text: It gives individuals over 13 (or their guardians) the right to request deletion of personal information collected about them while they were under 13, and requires websites to honor those requests and confirm deletion in writing.
It requires child-directed sites to post prominent notices explaining how to request deletion, so the right is not hidden.
It lets state attorneys general enforce the new deletion right, adding a layer of accountability beyond federal regulators.

analysis.who_pays: Websites and online services directed to children. They would have to build systems to accept deletion requests, verify the requester, actually delete the data (not just make it unretrievable in normal business), and confirm deletions in writing. Operators with actual knowledge they collected data from children would face the same duties even if their site is not aimed at kids.
analysis.who_pays_short: Websites and online services aimed at children

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: websites directed to children would have to build request systems, verify ages and identities, and delete data on demand, which is a real administrative burden especially for small operators.

The right is narrow: it covers only data collected by sites directed to children (or where the operator knew it was collecting from a child), so data gathered by general-audience platforms about minors would largely be out of scope.
Deletion is not absolute — operators may retain information needed for court processes or law-enforcement/public-safety investigations, so a full 'clean slate' is not guaranteed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — allowing adults to erase data profiles built on them as children — is real and targeted, and the narrow law-enforcement exception addresses the main safety objection. The main cost is compliance work for online services, which would likely be passed to consumers only marginally. The larger honest criticism is that the bill was narrow and went nowhere: it addresses only data collected before age 13, on child-directed sites, leaving most of the broader youth-data problem untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and sent it to the Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Durbin introduced the bill on February 13, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
No further action was ever taken — the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the committee or the Senate.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of child-directed websites keep the data they collected about children, with no deletion obligation. Families and young adults gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a deletion right for data collected from children, building on the 1998 children's privacy law he has long worked on.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill ended with only two cosponsors, both Democrats.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 13, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Online advertising and data-broker industry
against.what_they_did: Industry groups broadly oppose expanded deletion rights that would erase collected data, and such opposition is a routine presence in privacy debates; no specific lobbying on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship (three Democrats) and never advanced far enough for any vote that would show whether it split by party.

industries.industry: Websites and online services directed at children (and child-focused ad-tech)
industries.note: They would lose the ability to keep and reuse data collected about users when those users were children, and would bear the cost of building deletion-request and confirmation systems. Today they can retain that data indefinitely.

The bill amends existing children's privacy law rather than creating a broad new regime, but any platform with actual knowledge it collected data from children would face the same deletion obligations and enforcement exposure.
